overview: The Yamato period marks the emergence of a unified Japanese state centered in the Yamato region. Large keyhole-shaped burial mounds reflect the power of regional chiefs who gradually came under imperial authority.

items.text: Keyhole-shaped kofun burial mounds, some over 400 meters long, built for rulers.
Haniwa clay figurines placed on tomb mounds depict warriors, horses, houses and people.
Bronze mirrors and weapons imported from Korea and China.
Buddhism introduced from Baekje Korea, leading to debate between pro- and anti-Buddhist factions.
Native Shinto beliefs in spirits coexisted with imported Buddhism and Confucianism.
Iron tools and weapons production improved through Korean contacts.
Chinese writing system adopted for official records.
The imperial line established during this period continues to the present.
Kofun burial mounds remain prominent archaeological sites.

fall.text: The establishment of a permanent capital at Heijo-kyo in 710 marks the transition to the Nara period.
